title: The Friction Ledger: A Zero-Sum Accounting of Polymarket Order Flow and the Geometry of Event-Contract Fees
abstract: This paper asks where prediction-market money goes. A defined active-core sample of 1,338,933 Polymarket BUY-side fills across 439 settled markets contains $419.4 million of buy notional. Treating each BUY-side fill as taker-initiated because the public tape lacks a maker/taker flag, the ledger gives +0.143% gross selection, +1.488% modelled fees and -1.345% net. Fees are 10.4 times the gross edge. The modelled fee family r*p*(1-p) charges most at 50 cents and approaches zero near certainty. A floored curve, r'*p*max(1-p, m), is static-revenue-neutral on the calibration, cuts mid-range fees 25.9% at m = 0.20 and makes even a $1 payout unprofitable above 99.26 cents. The scenario-specific break-even response ratio is 0.60. A separate register contains 123,499 grouped UMA oracle records. Among groups with a settled dispute, 7.12% had at least one proposal change. Frozen aggregate snapshots are public. Their arithmetic can be checked; they do not reproduce the raw-tape analysis. AI disclosure: Claude prepared the initial publication drafts. OpenAI Codex assisted with editing, source checks, numerical consistency checks, an independent AI review and PDF preparation. AI output is not evidence. Ailin Sun is responsible for the manuscript. This working paper has not undergone external peer review.
why: Polymarket microstructure ($419M). Fee analysis, practical design.

title: Large Language Models, Price Discovery, and Synchronized Trading
abstract: (This paper is written by Jiawei Wang (Warwick Business School, University of Warwick).) Large language models lower the cost of reading corporate disclosures, but reliance on common models can also make investors’ interpretations more similar. I study this trade-off using the public launch of ChatGPT and three pre-launch properties of corporate filings: readability, length, and uncertainty. AI can help decode difficult prose, but it cannot resolve uncertainty about outcomes that the disclosure leaves unaddressed. After the launch, order flow becomes more one-sided in hard-to-read firms. The effect grows as frontier models accumulate and appears in both retail and non-retail trading. This greater synchronization also carries information. In these firms, weekly return reversal falls by about half, earnings news is incorporated faster, and synchronized order flow predicts returns at longer horizons. The effect also extends across stocks: non-retail order flow comoves more across hard-to-read stocks. Length has little stable relation with these outcomes, while uncertainty weakens synchronization without improving price discovery. To rationalize these patterns, I develop a Kyle-style model in which delegation improves decoding but introduces shared error. Because trading on information held by others is less profitable, delegation is a strategic substitute and crowding limits adoption. The model explains how greater synchronization can coexist with better price discovery.
why: ChatGPT impact on equity trading synchronization. Real data.

title: Calibration that counts: Conformal prediction intervals for automated valuation models
abstract: Automated valuation models (AVMs) increasingly determine the value of residential collateral in mortgage origination, collateral revaluation and capital regulation. The literature focuses on the accuracy of point predictions; the reliability of the intervals AVMs attach to those predictions remains largely unexplored. Using the complete transaction record of England and Wales (HM Land Registry linked to the Energy Performance Certificate register; 10,697,025 out-of-sample valuations in 2010–2026), we study the calibration of prediction intervals for three AVM classes — hedonic regression, gradient boosting and a neural network — under a strictly temporal protocol. The native intervals of all three classes are systematically miscalibrated, and the sign of the error differs across model classes: at a nominal 90% level, quantile boosting covers only 85.4% of realized prices while the neural network covers 92.3%. Plain conformal calibration reduces the error but leaves economically meaningful heterogeneity in coverage across price bands, regions and property types (a range of up to 12 percentage points) and fails at market breaks: during the 2022–2023 interest-rate shock, coverage of statically calibrated intervals falls to 77.9%. Mondrian (group-conditional) calibration equalizes coverage precisely along the dimension used for calibration, and adaptive quarterly recalibration keeps coverage at the nominal level throughout the break (89.7%). The gaps are economically material: the risk of a transaction price outside the reported range exceeds its nominal level by roughly half on average and more than doubles at the peak of the shock — exactly when collateral shortfalls materialize. Combining Mondrian and adaptive calibration yields intervals that are simultaneously calibrated, group-fair and robust to shocks — the properties supervisory frameworks demand of collateral valuation models but have so far been unable to enforce.
why: AVM calibration (10.6M transactions). Evaluation-focused, real problem.

title: Heterogeneity by Design for AI Liquidity Management Agents on Instant Payment Rails: A Conformance Specification
abstract: On a 24/7/365 instant payment rail such as FedNow, autonomous liquidity management agents observe the same public signals (overnight rates such as SOFR and intraday flow) and produce Liquidity Management Transfer (LMT) recommendations. If the population of agents shares one forecasting model and one decision rule, a single shock produces synchronized LMT requests in the same direction at the same time. This is herding, the model monoculture 1 risk identified by the Financial Stability Oversight Council in its 2024 Annual Report and kept under monitoring in its 2025 Annual Report. This specification defines three things: (i) a population-level herding index built from the net internal debt ∥δ∥ 1 of a payment network under a common rate shock; (ii) design requirements that keep agent behaviour heterogeneous across institutions by construction; and (iii) a conformance test that an institution or a service provider acting for many institutions can run to verify heterogeneity without disclosing proprietary models. The payment network and the net internal debt are taken from Martinez (2023); the rate-shock engine, a Hull-White short rate with a bounded deterministic perturbation, is taken from Martinez (2025). Heterogeneity is a property of the population, not of any single institution; it cannot be purchased by one participant alone. All thresholds in this version are provisional anda reference implementation reproduces every number reported here.
why: AI agents prevent herding on FedNow. FSOC-flagged risk.

title: Trade-Policy and Export-Control Exposure, Validated Textual Disclosure, and Capital-Market Outcomes
abstract: Do firms with material China and U.S. export-control exposure adequately disclose it, and does the gap predict capital-market consequences? I construct an exposure measure from Compustat geographic segment data, independent of filing text, and compare it to a validated text-mined disclosure measure combining a trade-policy-uncertainty co-occurrence rule (Caldara, Iacoviello, Molligo, Prestipino, & Raffo, 2020) and an export-control-specific keyword track validated against hand-labeled sentences using a large language model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct; 93.0% accuracy, F1 = 94.1%). An underdiscloser is a top-tercile-exposure firm-year with zero validated disclosure hits. Across three outcome tests (one-year-ahead crash risk, illiquidity, and an event study around the October 2022 Bureau of Industry and Security semiconductor export-control announcement), I find no robust evidence that underdisclosure predicts elevated crash risk, only a marginal, insignificant illiquidity association, and show that an apparently significant event-study result is an artifact of a two-firm sample that vanishes under proper power. The contribution is a rigorously validated disclosure-gap measure and a transparent null result.
why: Export-control disclosure doesn't predict prices. Real data.

title: When Does Reinforcement Learning Beat Naive Diversification? Learning Architecture, Regime Information, and Trading Frictions
abstract: This paper examines when reinforcement learning (RL) can outperform naive diversification in portfolio choice. We compare online actor-critic reinforcement learning with an offline Decision Transformer and the equally weighted 1/N benchmark, focusing on three determinants of outof-sample performance: learning architecture, regime information, and trading frictions. We find that conventional online actor-critic methods provide only modest improvements over 1/N , whereas the Decision Transformer delivers substantially stronger risk-adjusted performance. The value of regime information is non-monotonic: selected macroeconomic signals improve portfolio performance, but combining multiple regime-conditioning variables can materially reduce out-ofsample Sharpe ratios, consistent with an information-complexity tradeoff. These findings remain robust to alternative transaction-cost assumptions, and portfolio holdings reveal economically distinct allocation policies across architectures and information sets. Overall, reinforcement learning does not universally dominate naive diversification; its effectiveness depends critically on the interaction between learning architecture, state representation, and implementation frictions.
why: RL vs 1/N with proper baselines and costs.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Information Content of Financial Journalism
abstract: We examine the relation between generative AI assistance in professional financial journalism and news information content. We develop a paragraph-level AI detector using paired original and AI-polished Wall Street Journal articles, achieving a 96.45% F1 score on held-out test data. In 14,717 news observations from December 2022 through December 2025, articles classified as AI-assisted are associated with smaller absolute abnormal returns and lower abnormal trading volume around publication than articles not classified as AI-assisted. They also exhibit greater reading difficulty and lower frequencies of quantitative, earnings-related, and industry or economic content. Market-response attenuation is statistically significant among less experienced journalists. Journalists publish more articles and cover more firms after their first detected adoption of AI. These findings suggest that AI assistance accompanies greater journalistic output but less information conveyed to markets by each article.
why: AI detection in financial journalism (14K articles).

title: Do Policymakers Listen to Markets? Evidence from China's Industrial Policy Dismantling *
abstract: Do policymakers listen to stock markets when deciding which industries lose key policy support? We examine this question in the context of China's industrial policy dismantling across the 12th, 13th, and 14th Five-Year Plans (2011–2021). Dismantling refers to removing or downgrading an industry from key supported status. We identify dismantling by translating expert reading and keyword-matching procedures into structured large language model (LLM) prompts that rely on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Using probit models, we link pre-decision stock returns to the probability of dismantling. Industries with lower past cumulative returns (PastCR) during the information-gathering stage of policy drafting are significantly more likely to lose key support. This effect is stronger where public information is scarce, as in industries with limited media coverage and highly similar annual reports. These results are consistent with the view that stock prices convey complementary information rather than merely reflect common fundamentals. A Karlson–Holm–Breen decomposition attributes approximately one-tenth of the total effect to a reassessment of industry innovation capacity. Our results extend the price-informativeness literature to the policy domain. The proposed LLM-based approach provides a reproducible pipeline for extracting industry-level policy variables.
why: Solid LLM extraction for policy analysis; real data but incremental contribution

title: Socio-Spatial Graph Neural Networks for Financial Contagion Modeling and Explainable Default Risk Prediction
abstract: Traditional credit risk assessment commonly treats borrowers as independent tabular records, overlooking shared geographic and occupational stress that can produce correlated repayment outcomes. We present a reproducible socio-spatial dataset benchmark and testbed for explainable default risk prediction that represents borrowers as nodes in a structured relational network. The benchmark constructs weighted homophily links from observable pre-target attributes and derives structural centrality, community, and multi-hop neighborhood-stress features. A multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) learns relational representations that are exported to a downstream tree-based classifier, allowing graph signals to be compared with individual borrower attributes. We evaluate logistic, ensemble, graph feature proxy, and full graph feature models under a stratified protocol, and use ablation analysis to examine the contribution of relational information. The testbed provides a larger-scale experimental framework for studying graph construction, relational representation learning, downstream risk classification, explainability, and computational growth under a common reproducible pipeline. The framework also combines SHAP feature-group attribution with GAT edge attention to provide complementary global and relational explanations. A scalability analysis studies the computational behavior of the downstream evaluation as the benchmark grows. The results support controlled experiments in relational stress modeling while highlighting the limitations of synthetic data. The benchmark is not intended to establish causal contagion, demographic fairness, or regulatory compliance.
why: Network default risk. Solid, reproducible dataset.

title: Strategic Unreasonableness: A Tool of the Political Systematical Trader
abstract: This paper introduces strategic unreasonableness as a deliberate trading tool for situations where rational behavior has become predictable and therefore exploitable by AI trading systems. Drawing on game theory, military history, negotiation tactics, and business strategy, we establish strategic unreasonableness as a recognized phenomenon across domains. We then formalize the concept for trading and test it empirically using Monte Carlo simulation on SPY data (2015-2025) with a Donchian channel strategy. The results show that introducing 10-15% random deviation from rational behavior increases unpredictability to 0.97 (near maximum entropy) while reducing the Sharpe ratio by only 0.03. This holds even after accounting for 0.1% transaction costs per trade. The paper concludes that against pattern-learning AI adversaries, controlled randomness is not the absence of strategy-it is the optimal strategy for preserving edge while avoiding exploitation. AI Disclosure Statement: During the preparation of this work, the author used [Tool Name] for language polishing and grammar checking. After using this tool, the author reviewed and edited all content and takes full responsibility for the content of the publication.
why: Randomness in trading (SPY). Novel, limited scope.

title: Semantic Arbitrage and Feedback Instability in AI-to-AI Quotation Markets: Verified Generative Counterfactuals for Computational Theory
abstract: Enterprise procurement increasingly joins a buyer's generative-AI copilot with a seller's algorithmic quotation system. Although commercial requirements remain fixed, a copilot can express them through alternative request-for-quote documents that the seller interprets as different signals of urgency, switching costs, or willingness to pay. We define semantic arbitrage as the capture of quote dispersion across business-valid, truth-preserving representations of the same requirements. Historical transactions cannot identify this opportunity because each request usually reveals only one wording and one deployed price. We develop Verified Generative Counterfactuals (VGC), a generate-verify-probe-certify design that constructs the missing language interventions, audits semantic equivalence, randomizes or adaptively allocates quotation probes, and certifies the resulting operating regime. The buyer's optimal language policy has a Gibbs form. An exact value-risk identity shows that the same endogenous quote variance that creates procurement savings also generates feedback gain when the seller retrains on buyer-selected language. A unique equilibrium can therefore lose stability when gain and organizational latency cross an analytical boundary, producing endogenous quotation cycles and locally quadratic revenue loss. Semantic invariantization can guarantee stability, whereas batching may destabilize by increasing data age. A semi-synthetic study spanning 72 procurement records, 6,912 complete RFQs, four seller architectures, 400 paired search replications, and 1,584 delayed-system trajectories recovers the theoretical identities and stability frontier. The study validates the mechanism rather than estimating market prevalence. The findings connect digital representation, strategic interaction with algorithms, and performative organizational learning, while providing a rigorous, auditable governance framework for AI-mediated markets.
why: LLM RFQ generation for price discovery. Abstract incomplete.

title: AdaLogit: Oracle Credit Scoring via Adaptive Logistic Regression
abstract: We introduce AdaLogit, an adaptive logistic regression framework with elastic net regularization, which is particularly well suited to credit scoring applications. Unlike traditional ℓ p-regularized logistic regression, AdaLogit enjoys the oracle properties, ensuring consistent recovery of the true feature support even under complex correlation structures. Through a comprehensive empirical evaluation on synthetic and real-world credit scoring datasets, we show that AdaLogit matches or outperforms standard linear baselines while identifying significantly sparser and more stable feature sets. Compared with state-of-the-art blackbox classifiers such as TabPFN, AdaLogit approaches their predictive performance while remaining interpretable and providing better-calibrated probability estimates. For comparable balanced accuracy, AdaLogit often yields lower false negative rates than black-box alternatives. By preserving sharp tail probability calibration through oracle variable selection, this framework prioritizes default detection where error costs are highest, matching or exceeding the economic performance of TabPFN. The combination of transparency, stable feature selection and coefficient estimation, as well as accurate probability calibration, allows AdaLogit to decisively facilitate compliance with both the Basel Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) framework and the regulatory requirements of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act for high-risk AI systems.
why: Credit scoring with baseline, competent, single-country.

title: Between the Lines: Multi-turn Contextual Investment Advice Detection
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly power financial conversational assistants, detecting investment advice in natural language has become a critical regulatory and safety challenge. Unlike explicit single-turn recommendations, investment advice often emerges implicitly and progressively over multi-turn conversations, shaped by user intent, delivery style, and contextual buildup. We introduce the first comprehensive framework for detecting both sequential and contextual investment advice in dialogue settings. Central to our approach is a modular, top-down synthetic data generation pipeline that systematically spans a taxonomy of advisory trajectories using an axis-bucket-descriptor schema. We simulate both benign and high-risk conversations across diverse user personas, financial instruments, and risk tiers, and evaluate detection capabilities using LLM-as-a-Judge with entropy-based uncertainty diagnostics. Our results show that contextual advisory detection remains substantially more challenging than sequential cases, even under few-shot prompting with tailored demonstrations. This work lays the foundation for scalable guardrail development in highstakes, compliance-sensitive domains, where advisory risk is often subtle, distributed, and perception-dependent.
why: Investment advice detection (LLM, synthetic data).

title: From Predictive Models to Autonomous Market Intelligence
abstract: Research question. Can a financial AI system create more durable economic value when it is designed as a closedloop intelligence process-Observe-> Understand-> Predict-> Simulate-> Decide-> Measure-> Learn-> Predict Again-rather than as a one-shot stock-prediction model? This paper develops a conceptual and empirical framework for an Autonomous Financial Market Intelligence System (AFMIS), defined as a risk-governed computational system that continuously transforms heterogeneous market observations into probabilistic beliefs, stress-tested actions, realized-outcome measurements, and controlled model updates. The central claim is not that autonomous agents can reliably predict markets; rather, it is that the scientific object of study should be the quality of the entire forecast-to-decision learning loop. The framework integrates multimodal data ingestion, state estimation, ensemble forecasting, counterfactual simulation, decision optimization, online measurement, regimeaware memory, and model-promotion governance. It explicitly separates epistemic uncertainty from decision uncertainty and distinguishes predictive accuracy from economic utility. The paper contributes five elements. (1) a formal partially observed control formulation for autonomous financial intelligence; (2) a layered architecture that combines specialist forecasting models with agentic reasoning without allowing language models to become an ungoverned source of execution logic; (3) a "closed-loop advantage" hypothesis that makes continuous learning itself testable; (4) an empirical protocol based on rolling, embargoed, cost-aware evaluation, regime holdouts, simulation, calibration, and live shadow deployment; and (5) governance principles for memory, abstention, model promotion, auditability, and human override. The proposed research agenda is designed for a rigorous evaluation on liquid equity universes such as the NIFTY 500 and Russell 1000, while remaining generalizable to other asset classes. The paper is deliberately a framework and research design, not a claim of achieved alpha. Any implementation should be judged by net-of-cost out-of-sample performance, forecast calibration, drawdown and tail-risk behavior, robustness under regime shifts, and reproducibility. This distinction is essential because recent literature demonstrates both promising performance from AI-driven investment processes and substantial risks from information leakage, backtest overfitting, non-stationarity, and evaluation incomparability.
why: Closed-loop market intelligence. Conceptual framing, no validation.

title: A Regime-Aware, Free-Boundary Framework for Statistical Arbitrage: Kalman-Filtered Synthetic Baskets, EGARCH Volatility, Markov Regime Detection, and Optimal Stopping via Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman
abstract: We propose a statistical arbitrage framework for equity pairs and small synthetic baskets that replaces the conventional fixed-window z-score trading rule with a sequence of estimated stochastic models, each addressing a specific weakness of the standard approach. A synthetic long/short basket is constructed from Johansen cointegration loadings, restricted to the two largest-magnitude long and short weights per cluster on stability and significance grounds. The basket's hedge ratio is tracked with a Kalman filter rather than re-estimated by rolling OLS. The resulting spread's conditional volatility is modeled with an asymmetric EGARCH(1,1) process. A two-state Markov-switching model, informed by a small set of documented macro structural breaks (the 2020 COVID-19 liquidity shock and the 2024 AI-capex repricing / yen-carry unwind), gates trading activity to periods in which the spread is statistically behaving as mean-reverting. Entry and exit levels are not fixed multiples of a rolling standard deviation; they are the free boundaries of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck optimal stopping problem, solved via its Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman variational-inequality formulation with smooth-pasting conditions. A monthly seasonality overlay, shrunk toward a common prior via an empirical-Bayes (James-Stein) estimator and filtered through Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate control, acts as a veto rather than an independent signal. Capital is allocated across simultaneously active spreads via a mean-variance efficient frontier (GMV/MSR), scaled by an EGARCH-based dynamic Value-at-Risk. We present the full mathematical derivation, a from-scratch numerical implementation (Kalman recursion, EGARCH quasi-MLE, Hamilton-filter EM, Engle-Granger rolling cointegration, and a scipy.integrate.solve bvp-based free-boundary solver), and a synthetic validation study confirming that the regime filter correctly de-weights the two targeted structuralbreak windows.
why: Stat arb method (Kalman, EGARCH). No empirical results.

title: Artificial Intelligence, specialized assets and corporate diversification
abstract: Drawing on the knowledge-based view, this study examines the impact of AI innovation on corporate diversification decisions. Using a sample of U.S.-listed firms from 2010 to 2022, we document that AI innovation leads to a significant reduction in corporate diversification, driving firms toward greater strategic focus. To establish causality, we exploit two exogenous shocks: the 2016 deep learning breakthrough and the staggered adoption of state-level AI legislation. Mechanism tests reveal that AI innovation reduces diversification incentives by enhancing asset specificity through specialized asset investment and human capital specificity. In addition, the main effect is more pronounced among firms with shorter cash conversion cycles, smaller size, lower AI intensity, and headquartered in non-high-tech states. Overall, our findings highlight AI innovation as a vital driver of corporate specialization and provide novel insight into how emerging technologies reshape corporate boundaries, investment decisions, and resource allocation.
why: AI impact on diversification via causal shocks; corporate strategy not trading

title: Optimizing credit card limits: An explainable AI framework for Vietnamese commercial banks
abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has attracted considerable attention from scholars worldwide. However, while most existing studies focus on credit default classification or loan approval, credit card limit optimization remains relatively underexplored. This study aims to propose a credit limit prediction model that can utilize multidimensional data to improve the accuracy of customer assessment and integrate XAI techniques to provide transparent explanations of the model’s decision-making process. The empirical dataset consists of 82,483 observations with 21 variables, extracted from a commercial bank in Vietnam over the period from 2021 to 2025. The empirical results show that Gradient Boosting-based machine learning models achieve strong predictive performance, with AUC values above 0.94, among which XGBoost is selected as the optimal model. SHAP analysis confirms that the model’s decisions are not random but reflect traditional principles of credit risk management, with education level, financial capacity, and income being the most influential factors in credit limit decisions. Based on these findings, the study proposes several important policy implications for commercial banks in Vietnam.
why: Credit limits (XAI). Practical, not core focus.

title: Proof-Based Pricing: Why Unverified Claims Are Worth Nothing to an Algorithmic Buyer
abstract: Pricing theory has, until now, been written for a buyer who can be persuaded. Its three orientations, cost-based, competition-based, and customer value-based, differ in what they anchor a price to but agree on who reads it: a human who can be informed, framed, and convinced. In a growing, new class of consumer markets the reader is an AI agent that admits, verifies, and computes under an evaluation rule set by an intermediary, and the seller's claims reach that rule, not a person. This note defines Proof-Based Pricing: a seller-side pricing model for this configuration, in which the seller decides which claims to substantiate, how to make an offer eligible, and how to price when a delegated buyer applies an externally specified evaluation rule. The premise, that an algorithmic buyer discounts what it cannot verify and rewards what it can, was first set out in the author's book The Algorithmic Shopper (manuscript registered with the US Copyright Office in July 2025; St. Martin's Press, 2027); the pricing model itself is defined here. The closest formal ancestor is the procurement scoring auction, in which a buyer selects among bids under a published rule; Proof-Based Pricing adapts that selection to consumer markets in three structural ways: the evaluation rule is set by an intermediary exogenous to both sides; admission turns on the machine legibility of the offer; and the seller responds with a published price schedule on verifiable attributes rather than a bid. We characterize acceptance by the proof coefficient, the agent's posterior expected value relative to the schedule price: an admitted offer is acceptable exactly when the coefficient is at least the intermediary's price weight, with equality for the marginal offer. We state five falsifiable propositions with the observation that would refute each, set out a measurement agenda with named test beds, and specify the first experiment.
why: Pricing for algorithmic buyers. Position paper.

title: Kinetopus Engine: A Parsimonious Physical-Mathematical Pipeline for Local-First Financial Time Series Forecasting using Sparse Identification of Dynamical Systems (SINDy)
abstract: Financial time series analysis has long been trapped in a dichotomy between linear, oversimplified statistical models (e.g., ARIMA) and opaque, computationally expensive deep learning black boxes (e.g., LSTMs, Transformers). This paper introduces Kinetopus Engine, a parsimonious, White-Box Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) framework that challenges the assumption of pure stochastic randomness by constructing a mathematically justified continuous physical perspective over discrete financial data. Operating under low computational complexity on consumer-grade CPU hardware (≤ 16 GB RAM), the pipeline integrates five core stages: (1) Spectral sensing via Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to detect dominant cyclical frequencies; (2) Topological manifold smoothing via C 2 Splines to reconstruct continuous price-volume trajectories; (3) Online Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) control mechanisms for real-time structural regime-shift slicing; (4) Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) to discover explicit, parsimonious ordinary differential equations dr/dt = f (r, V); and (5) Probabilistic Monte Carlo trajectory projection via Euler-Maruyama stochastic differential equations (SDEs) stabilized by a hydrodynamic friction regularizer (λ = 0.99). Empirical evaluation through an extensive walk-forward benchmark encompassing 3,525 evaluation iterations across a heterogeneous six-asset universe (BTC-USD, ETH-USD, MSFT, QQQ, XLF, GLD) demonstrates a sustained aggregate directional Hit Ratio of 59.15% at a 150-candle horizon (∼ 7.5 months), achieving strong statistical significance against a random-walk null hypothesis (z = 4.942, p
why: Price predictor, no baseline or transaction costs shown.

title: GL-Agent: Security Investment under Capability Tax, Adaptive Defence, and Control Displacement
abstract: Security controls for AI agents can reduce successful attacks while also reducing useful capability, exhausting intervention capacity, or displacing activity into less-governed channels. A decision rule based only on breach-probability reduction can therefore recommend the wrong control intensity or portfolio. This paper develops GL-Agent, an extension of the Gordon-Loeb investment framework that distinguishes attack success, conditional severity, loss-weighted intervention effectiveness, delivered benefit, direct cost, and control-induced displacement. Its principal result is an over-control theorem with bounded migration: even when governed risk falls exponentially and substitute usage cannot exceed the available workload, realized risk can have a unique interior minimum and rise thereafter. The welfare optimum occurs earlier when the marginal control burden is positive. A more general ordering result does not require a convex risk trajectory. For a restricted exponential-loss family, an all-in investment bound of 1/𝑒 survives heterogeneous action classes, multiple control instruments, and convex burden accounting; it is not a universal budget rule for the full model. Further results clarify durabilityadjusted control value, the assumptions behind a common-mode failure ceiling, and why dependence alone does not invalidate submodular portfolio selection. An independently implemented numerical supplement reproduces the model and identifies both single-and multiple-peak regimes. A measurement protocol and proposed experiments address semantic manipulation of summaries and delegated tool authority. No new field or model-evaluation data are reported. The contribution is a conditional theory and reproducible decision framework, with empirical claims explicitly separated from mathematical results and synthetic illustrations.
why: Security investment theory. Pure theory, no implementation.

title: BayesShield-Driven Uncertainty Quantification in Encrypted Cross-Bank Credit Assessments
abstract: The increasing adoption of collaborative machine learning in the financial sector, particularly for cross-bank credit risk assessment, is severely hampered by two critical challenges: the stringent regulatory requirements for data privacy and the inherent unpredictability of model predictions in high-stakes lending decisions. While homomorphic encryption (HE) offers a pathway to perform computations on encrypted data, safeguarding client confidentiality, it introduces significant computational overhead and complicates the deployment of complex, uncertainty-aware models. Existing privacy-preserving frameworks often prioritize security over interpretability, leaving financial institutions unable to quantify the confidence of their credit decisions, thereby undermining risk management and regulatory compliance. This research introduces BayesShield, a novel framework that synergistically integrates Bayesian neural networks with advanced cryptographic protocols to enable robust uncertainty quantification (UQ) within fully encrypted cross-bank credit assessment environments. BayesShield is architected to operate directly on HE-encrypted client features, employing a scalable, deterministic approximation of Bayesian inference-such as Monte Carlo Dropout or a Laplace approximation-to generate predictive distributions without decrypting the underlying data. Our framework comprises three core innovations: (1) a precision-optimized neural network architecture that minimizes multiplicative depth to reduce HE computational latency; (2) a novel entropy-based metric for decomposing predictive uncertainty into its aleatoric (data-inherent) and epistemic (model-knowledge) components from encrypted logits; and (3) a distributed consensus protocol for aggregating encrypted uncertainties from multiple participating banks, ensuring that no single entity can access individual client data or model gradients. Through comprehensive empirical evaluation on synthetic and real-world credit default datasets, we demonstrate that BayesShield achieves comparable predictive performance to non-private Bayesian models while providing actionable uncertainty estimates. Critically, we show that the privacy-preserving UQ enables the early detection of out-of-distribution applicants and model drift, thereby alerting risk officers to potentially unreliable decisions without compromising client privacy. Our results indicate that the framework's computational overhead is feasible for practical deployment, offering a latency reduction of approximately 35% compared to naive HE-Bayesian implementations. By delivering verifiable and interpretable risk metrics in a privacy-preserving manner, BayesShield establishes a new paradigm for secure, trustworthy, and transparent collaborative credit scoring, fostering greater inter-institutional cooperation while adhering to the principles of GDPR, CCPA, and other data protection regulations.
why: Encrypted credit assessment. Conceptual only.

title: The Auditor's Dilemma: Verifying Encrypted Credit Models While Preserving Secrecy
abstract: The increasing adoption of machine learning in credit scoring offers significant advantages in predictive accuracy and efficiency but introduces a critical governance challenge: the "Auditor's Dilemma." Regulatory mandates for model explainability, fairness, and robustness necessitate rigorous third-party audits, yet these audits conflict with the proprietary nature of the models and the stringent privacy requirements of the underlying financial data. This research addresses the fundamental tension between verifiability and secrecy by exploring the application of advanced cryptographic techniques-specifically secure multi-party computation (MPC), fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), and zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs)-to enable confidential model auditing. We propose a novel framework that allows an external auditor to perform substantive testing on an encrypted credit model and its private data inputs without decrypting either, thereby ensuring the model's performance, bias, and compliance are validated without compromising business secrets or customer privacy. Our approach includes a protocol for verifying algorithmic fairness on encrypted demographic data, a method for assessing model robustness to adversarial inputs via encrypted perturbation, and a mechanism for generating publicly verifiable, non-interactive proofs of audit results. The findings demonstrate that while cryptographic overhead imposes computational costs, our framework achieves a viable balance between security and utility, offering a pragmatic pathway for financial institutions to satisfy regulatory requirements and build public trust while safeguarding their intellectual property and sensitive information. This work contributes a foundational architecture for the next generation of privacy-preserving financial audits, effectively resolving the auditor's dilemma by proving, rather than revealing, the integrity of the model.
why: Cryptographic auditing framework. Conceptual, no results.

title: Integrating LLMs into R Shiny-based Risk Management Applications
abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into institutional risk management workflows represents a pivotal transition from static, report-driven decision support towards dynamic, context-aware analytical environments. This paper introduces a practitioner-developed, step-by-step reference architecture for embedding retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agentic LLM workflows into R Shiny-based risk management applications within a regulated European banking institution. This paper is an extension of the framework for R Shiny-based risk management applications as described in Lovrić (2023) [9]. To our knowledge, this is the first paper focusing on a step-by-step approach for integrating LLMs into risk management applications and workflows of European banks.
why: R Shiny LLM integration guide; tutorial not research

title: Risk-Based Approaches in Anti-Money Laundering for Balancing Regulatory Compliance Costs and Maximizing Detection of High-Risk Financial Activities
abstract: This study explores risk-based approaches (RBAs) in anti-money laundering (AML) frameworks, aiming to balance regulatory compliance costs with effective detection of high-risk financial activities. Utilizing a mixedmethods research design, the study analyzes datasets from financial institutions and regulatory reports, employing statistical tools and machine learning algorithms to evaluate RBA efficacy. Findings indicate that RBAs reduce compliance costs by 15-20% compared to traditional rule-based systems while improving detection rates of suspicious transactions by 25%. Key challenges include data quality and regulatory ambiguity. The study concludes that RBAs offer a scalable solution for AML compliance, provided institutions invest in advanced analytics and training. Recommendations include harmonizing global RBA guidelines and enhancing public-private data-sharing mechanisms to strengthen AML frameworks.
why: AML cost reduction claims on synthetic data.

title: Graph-Based Network Analysis for Identifying Complex Money Laundering Typologies, Detecting Suspicious Transaction Chains, and Tracing Illicit Financial Flows
abstract: This study explores the application of graph-based network analysis to combat money laundering by identifying complex typologies, detecting suspicious transaction chains, and tracing illicit financial flows. Utilizing hypothetical yet realistic financial transaction datasets, the research employs graph theory, machine learning algorithms, and network visualization tools to model and analyze transactional relationships. The findings reveal that graph-based methods effectively uncover hidden patterns, such as layered transactions and circular flows, with high precision. Two tables and two charts illustrate key metrics, including node centrality and clustering coefficients. The study underscores the potential of graph analytics to enhance anti-money laundering (AML) frameworks, offering actionable insights for financial institutions and regulators. However, limitations such as data quality and computational scalability are noted. Future research should focus on integrating real-time data and advanced anomaly detection to strengthen AML efforts.
why: Graph AML on synthetic data, unvalidated.

title: Applying Financial Transaction-Monitoring Analytics to Pharmaceutical and Precursor-Chemical Import Screening: A Framework for Data-Driven Regulatory Risk Management
abstract: The 2026 National Drug Control Strategy identifies fragmented, siloed data systems and limited analytical capacity as structural weaknesses in the U.S. government's ability to screen and monitor pharmaceutical and precursor-chemical imports, and calls for modernized, standardized data systems and expanded risk-based screening. For a structurally similar problem, financial institutions have spent twenty years developing a nearly identical capability: identifying anomalous cross-border transactions, reconciling multi-jurisdiction compliance documentation, monitoring exception rates against specified KPIs and SLAs, and scoring a transaction using its own financial attributes, corridor, counterparty, payment memo, structuring pattern, under Bank Secrecy Act and anti-money-laundering (AML) regimes. This paper argues that the toolkit is directly transferable to pharmaceutical and precursor-chemical import screening using a structured cross-domain mapping methodology, treating financial-crimes transaction monitoring as the source domain and pharmaceutical/precursor-chemical import screening as the target domain. It proposes a framework based on five components, three of which are expressed as named, itemized scores: a Trade Risk Score built from the shipment's own declared attributes against the importer's baseline, a Documentation Risk Score built from cross-system completeness and consistency, a Financial Risk Score built from the payment's own financial attributes origin, beneficiary, corridor, third-party payer, timing, counterparty history, joined to the shipment via a shared invoice or purchase-order reference where available, or through entity resolution otherwise, an entity-resolution layer linking importer, exporter, financial-counterparty, and beneficial-owner identities across filings and payments, and KPI/SLA-based exception dashboards. The three scores combine into a single Integrated Import Risk Score, mirroring the composite fraud-and-AML scorecards banks already run. The study examines FinCEN's own Bank Secrecy Act data mining on fentanyl-related illicit finance, which in 2024 identified about $1.4 billion in suspected transactions with distinguishable wire-corridor, payment-memo, and shell-company typologies. This is not done as a distant analogy, but rather as proof of the financial-transaction signals that the Financial Risk Score would try to include, joined when feasible to shipment-side declarations. It shows how the shipment-side components could be layered onto existing infrastructure, CBP's Automated Commercial Environment, FDA's PREDICT risk-targeting system, and the INCB's PEN Online precursor pre-export notification system, in a way that could potentially leverage existing statutory and reporting infrastructure, subject to agency-specific legal and governance review, while the financial-data-integration component would require a legally authorized interagency data-sharing mechanism between Treasury/FinCEN and the trade agencies; this paper does not determine whether additional statutory or regulatory authority would be required. The paper situates its contribution against the closest existing research, including the NSF-funded FIND-M project and a broader academic literature on trade-based money laundering, financial-crime analytics, explainable AI, illicit-supply-chain networks, counterfeit medicines, and data-driven customs risk management, and identifies the specific gap in that literature its framework addresses. It concludes with the framework's implications for regulators and industry compliance teams and identifies what would be needed to test it against real institutional data.
why: Transfer AML to pharma imports. Position paper.

title: Deepfake Fraud in Digital Banking: Using Artificial Intelligence to Strengthen Fraud Detection and Identity Verification
abstract: Deepfake fraud is rapidly emerging as an existential threat to digital banking ecosystems, fueled by unprecedented advancements in generative artificial intelligence, synthetic media, and voice cloning algorithms. Cybercriminals increasingly leverage hyper-realistic face-swapping, deepfake video injection, and acoustic speech synthesis to bypass conventional Know-Your-Customer (KYC) protocols, biometric authentication systems, and remote onboarding frameworks. Despite vast literature on financial cybersecurity, traditional research primarily targets transactional anomalies, network intrusion, and static credential fraud, leaving significant vulnerabilities in dynamic, AI-driven identity spoofs. This study introduces a comprehensive, multimodal AI-driven framework designed to integrate multi-factor synthetic media detection into digital banking risk engines. By contextualizing facial biomechanics, vocal frequencies, dynamic behavioral biometrics, and transactional telemetry within an Explainable AI (XAI) architecture, the proposed model evaluates identity risk in real-time. Additionally, a mixedmethod empirical methodology-combining expert qualitative insights, quantitative user surveys, and benchmark evaluation across XGBoost, ResNet-50, and Transformer architectures-is presented. Special contextual emphasis is placed on emerging markets like Pakistan, where digital financial inclusion is accelerating rapidly amidst evolving regulatory oversight.
why: Deepfake fraud security, not core financial market work.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Fintech-Enabled Financial Inclusion: A Comparative Analysis of Bias and Explainability in Global and Indian Regulatory Frameworks
abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into financial technology has significantly expanded the frontiers of financial inclusion. However, this has also led to governance challenges that existing regulatory frameworks need to adapt to. This research investigates the impact of AI in financial technology and focuses on the challenges emerging from its deployment in ensuring financial inclusion. It then analyses two critical policy challenges: embedded bias and the lack of explainability in AI systems. The paper conducts a comparative analysis of global frameworks such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, and the European Union AI Act and further evaluates India's regulatory landscape of MEITY advisories and SEBI guidelines. Finally it provides recommendations that ensure robust AI governance by removing bias, upholding consumer rights, and guaranteeing algorithmic explainability and accountability.
why: Regulatory framework survey, rejected as literature review.

title: When Everyone Has an Excavator: How AI Changes Comparative Advantage in Accounting Research
abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping the production function of empirical accounting research. Using a conceptual production-function framework, I argue that generative AI lowers the cost of execution-intensive tasks, including coding, data cleaning, text processing, documentation, diagnostics, and first-pass implementation of unfamiliar methods. AI does not make research judgment less important. It makes judgment more important by lowering the relative value of routine execution and raising the relative value of question selection, institutional knowledge, economic intuition, research design, and skepticism. The result is a partial leveling of the empirical research playing field, but not a complete one. Proprietary data, training, networks, time, and the ability to evaluate AI output remain important sources of inequality. Accounting researchers, doctoral programs, reviewers, and editors should place greater weight on where researchers choose to dig, not merely how quickly or impressively they do so.
why: Position paper on AI changing research production

title: Minimum Necessary Intervention: Constraint-Based Adaptive Assistance with Intervention Debt and Recovery-Aware Withdrawal
abstract: Artificial intelligence can improve task completion, yet stronger assistance can also reduce opportunities for independent recovery. We present Minimum Necessary Intervention (MNI), a control framework that treats assistance as a graded resource rather than a binary feature. MNI estimates user struggle, predicts recovery across an ordered intervention ladder, selects the least costly action satisfying a recovery-probability constraint, verifies recovery, escalates only when necessary, and withdraws support following recovery. We operationalize Intervention Debt as intervention burden weighted by the absence of modeled independent recovery. A reproducible synthetic benchmark spanning six digital-use domains compares MNI with no assistance, static help, and maximum assistance. Across 20 random seeds with 1,200 users per seed, MNI achieved mean completion of 0.703 (95% CI [0.698, 0.709]) with mean intervention burden of 0.632, compared with 0.769 completion and 1.000 burden under maximum assistance. MNI reduced modeled Intervention Debt from 0.785 to 0.443 and increased modeled independent recovery from 0.215 to 0.392 relative to maximum assistance. Pareto, longitudinal, ablation, heterogeneity, domain-shift, sensing-noise, and adversarial stress tests reveal a consistent trade-off rather than universal dominance. These results support MNI as a recovery-aware framework for providing sufficient assistance without defaulting to maximal automation.
why: Adaptive assistance framework. Non-financial domain.

title: Predictive Analytics in Anti-Money Laundering for Detecting High-Frequency Trading Abuses and Identifying Early Warning Signs of Financial Crime
abstract: This study explores the application of predictive analytics in anti-money laundering (AML) frameworks to detect high-frequency trading (HFT) abuses and identify early warning signs of financial crime. By leveraging machine learning algorithms and big data analytics, the research analyzes transactional datasets to uncover patterns indicative of illicit activities. The methodology integrates supervised and unsupervised learning models, utilizing hypothetical yet realistic financial datasets from global trading platforms. Findings reveal that predictive models achieve up to 85% accuracy in detecting HFT-related money laundering, with key indicators including abnormal trade volumes and rapid transaction sequences. The study underscores the potential of predictive analytics to enhance regulatory compliance and mitigate financial crime risks. Implications for policymakers and financial institutions include improved detection systems and proactive risk management. Limitations, such as data quality and model interpretability, are discussed, alongside future research directions.
why: Predictive AML/HFT. Synthetic data, no validation.

title: Integration of Biometric Authentication with AML Systems for Strengthening Know-Your-Customer (KYC) Processes and Reducing Identity Fraud in Financial Institutions
abstract: This study explores the integration of biometric authentication with anti-money laundering (AML) systems to enhance Know-Your-Customer (KYC) processes and mitigate identity fraud in financial institutions. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach, the research analyzes hypothetical datasets from banking environments, employing statistical tools and machine learning algorithms to evaluate system efficacy. Findings indicate that biometric-AML integration reduces identity fraud by 32% and improves KYC compliance rates by 28%, with facial recognition and fingerprint scanning showing superior accuracy. The study highlights challenges, including data privacy concerns and implementation costs, but underscores significant improvements in security and operational efficiency. Policy implications suggest standardized frameworks for biometric data use, while future research is recommended to address scalability and cross-border regulatory alignment. This research contributes to the evolving discourse on technological interventions in financial security, offering actionable insights for practitioners and regulators.
why: Biometric-AML on hypothetical data, unvalidated.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Powered Anti-Money Laundering Framework for Enhancing Suspicious Transaction Detection, Automating Compliance Processes, and Strengthening Fraud Prevention in Financial Institutions
abstract: This study proposes an innovative Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered framework designed to bolster anti-money laundering (AML) efforts within financial institutions. The primary aim is to address persistent challenges in suspicious transaction detection, compliance automation, and fraud prevention amid escalating global financial crimes. Employing a mixed-methods approach, the research leverages synthetic datasets mimicking real-world transaction patterns and advanced machine learning algorithms, including deep neural networks and graph-based anomaly detection. Key findings reveal that the proposed framework achieves a 92% accuracy rate in identifying suspicious activities, reducing false positives by 45% compared to traditional rule-based systems, and automating 78% of compliance reporting processes. These outcomes underscore the framework's efficacy in enhancing operational efficiency and regulatory adherence. In conclusion, the integration of AI not only fortifies financial integrity but also offers scalable solutions for resource-constrained institutions, paving the way for proactive risk mitigation in an era of sophisticated cyber threats
why: AI-AML on synthetic data, inflated accuracy.

title: Integration of Blockchain with Artificial Intelligence for Developing Trustworthy Predictive Analytics Models in Financial Transactions and Detecting Fraudulent Activities through Decentralized Learning Frameworks
abstract: This study explores the integration of blockchain technology with artificial intelligence (AI) to develop trustworthy predictive analytics models for financial transactions and detect fraudulent activities through decentralized learning frameworks. By leveraging blockchain's immutable ledger and AI's predictive capabilities, the research addresses trust, transparency, and security challenges in financial systems. A mixed-methods approach was employed, analyzing hypothetical yet realistic financial transaction datasets using federated learning algorithms and blockchain-based smart contracts. Findings indicate that decentralized frameworks enhance model accuracy by 15% and reduce fraud detection latency by 20% compared to centralized systems. The study highlights improved trust through transparent data sharing and identifies scalability as a key limitation. These results contribute to advancing secure, scalable financial systems, with implications for policy and practice in digital finance.
why: Blockchain-AI federated learning, vague contribution.

title: A Blockchain-Enabled Real-Time Fraud Detection Framework for Financial Institutions Leveraging AI-Powered Risk Assessment and Tamper-Proof Transaction Auditing
abstract: This study proposes a novel blockchain-enabled framework integrating artificial intelligence (AI) for real-time fraud detection in financial institutions. By combining AI-powered risk assessment with tamper-proof transaction auditing on a blockchain, the framework addresses escalating fraud challenges in digital banking. The methodology employs a hybrid dataset of transactional records, machine learning algorithms, and a permissioned blockchain for secure auditing. Key findings reveal a 92% accuracy in fraud detection, a 35% reduction in false positives, and enhanced audit reliability. The framework outperforms traditional systems in speed and transparency, offering scalable solutions for financial security. Implications include improved regulatory compliance and customer trust. Limitations involve computational costs and blockchain scalability. Future research should explore quantum-resistant blockchains and federated learning. This study contributes to the convergence of AI and blockchain for robust financial systems.
why: Blockchain fraud detection. Likely synthetic data.

title: Dynamic Deficit-Triggered Capacity Control for AI Compute Infrastructure: A Lead-Time-Aware Stochastic Framework with Elastic Capacity and Adaptive Bayesian Portfolio Control
abstract: AI compute infrastructure requires capital-intensive capacity decisions under rapidly changing and uncertain demand, long procurement and construction lead times, and increasing availability of elastic rented capacity. This paper develops a computational framework termed Dynamic Deficit-Triggered Capacity Control (DDTCC). The central hypothesis is that irreversible physical expansion should be triggered by the expected capacity deficit at the time when newly ordered capacity becomes operational, rather than by an undifferentiated forecast of future demand. Five capacity-control policies are evaluated with common random numbers. Four are fixed decision rules-aggressive forecast-based expansion, fixed-threshold deficit-driven expansion, risk-aware control, and a hybrid physical-plus-elastic policy-and, across 4,000 paths over 120 months, attain mean discounted costs of 1773.36, 2718.19, 1757.53, and 751.04 normalized units per path, respectively. The fifth policy, Adaptive Portfolio Control (AP-DDTCC), combines four mechanisms that extend the fixed-rule controllers: (i) online Bayesian estimation of the demand growth rate via a local-level Kalman filter, replacing the assumption that the controller knows the true drift; (ii) dual-horizon deficit thresholds tuned online by a Robbins-Monro stochasticapproximation rule that targets a pre-specified service level instead of using a fixed threshold; (iii) pipeline-aware deficit accounting, which nets out capacity already ordered but not yet commissioned, correcting a source of overordering present in the fixed-threshold controllers; and (iv) a three-tier capacity portfolio (long-lead physical capacity, a medium-lead reservedcapacity class, and instantaneous elastic capacity) that generalizes the scalar capacity variable of the fixed-rule model to a vector of resource classes. On the identical demand paths used for the four-policy comparison, Adaptive Portfolio Control attains a mean discounted cost of 616.85 normalized units with full simulated service (service level 1.0), a paired reduction of 134.19 normalized units relative to the hybrid policy (95% bootstrap CI: 104.39-156.60; Cohen's d =-0.16; lower cost on 78.45% of paths) and of 1156.51 units relative to aggressive expansion (95% CI: 1084.81-1229.19). Global variance-based (Sobol) screening attributes the majority of Adaptive Portfolio cost variance in the tested domain to demand jump probability (total-order index 0.675) and capacity lead time (0.334), with reserved-capacity lead time and elastic price contributing negligibly. Robustness checks across an extended range of elastic-capacity prices show the Adaptive Portfolio policy remains the lowest-cost option up to an elastic price of approximately 5.2-5.3 normalized units per unit of capacity, beyond which its advantage over static risk-aware control erodes. The computational experiment uses synthetic demand generated by a fully specified stochastic process; no company-specific observations are used and no synthetic quantity 1 is represented as empirical evidence. All reported figures are generated directly from the accompanying code with a fixed random seed. The principal scientific contribution is not a claim that any one policy is universally optimal, but a falsifiable, reproducible control architecture that couples expansion timing to lead-time-adjusted, online-recalibrated deficit risk, and that treats capacity as a portfolio of resources with heterogeneous lead times and costs rather than a single irreversible commitment. The manuscript specifies the model, algorithms, tests, uncertainty analysis, sensitivity analysis, limitations, and reproducibility artifacts required for independent examination.
why: Off-topic: AI infrastructure capacity planning, not financial work.

title: The Missing First Rung: Aggregate Resilience and Entry-Level Compression in the AI Labor Market
abstract: Public discussion of artificial intelligence and employment has split between a jobs apocalypse and an AI jobs boom. Both claims are easier to make than to count because creation is often measured with broad infrastructure employment while displacement is restricted to explicitly attributed layoffs. I construct a symmetric occupation-industry ledger from Current Population Survey microdata covering January 2015 through August 2026. The primary universe fully excludes electric-power cells; power appears only in a separate sensitivity analysis. I also formalize a demand-expansion mechanism in which AI can increase output while reducing the junior labor required per unit of output. Aggregate results show resilience rather than collapse, but not a model-invariant boom. In an observed-use design, the post-ChatGPT aggregate high-exposure employment gap ranges from minus 0.47 to plus 0.34 percentage points across four counterfactuals. Its first-year gap lies 0.009 points above the maximum of five post hoc fully pre-pandemic placebo windows, but the five-window comparison has a minimum attainable randomization p value of 0.167; the gap also lies inside the wider distribution formed by eight pre-event breaks, three of which overlap the pandemic. The latest broad occupation-industry balance is 0.52 to 0.97 million jobs above trend, but its post-event mean ranges from minus 0.25 to plus 0.12 million. For workers age 22 to 25, high observed-exposure employment is 2.19 to 2.58 percentage points below trend across specifications; the primary estimate is minus 2.58 points. Their probability of moving from nonemployment into any job is 4.30 points below trend in the primary model and remains negative under all four counterfactuals. I read this as first-rung compression within a broader and partly model-dependent youth employment slowdown, not as a pure AI substitution effect. Ages 26 to 35 have negative average stock gaps in three of four counterfactuals and negative cell-ledger balances in all four, so they are not a clean unaffected control. The bottom line is aggregate resilience with a pronounced first-rung compression whose exact causal AI share remains unidentified.
why: AI labor displacement (CPS). Economics, off-topic.

title: A Public Debt Reduction Plan for the United Kingdom
abstract: In 2025-26 the United Kingdom spent £96.9 billion on central government net debt interest on the Office for National Statistics measure, and £109.7 billion on the Office for Budget Responsibility measure. The OBR forecasts £137.1 billion by 2030-31. Debt interest is the second largest item of public spending and the only one that funds no public service. Three things drive the bill. Index-linked gilts stood at £672.7 billion in uplifted nominal value at 31 March 2026, 23.9 per cent of the portfolio, the highest share in the G7 and about twice the next highest. Central bank reserves, which averaged £664.9 billion in 2025-26, earn Bank Rate, so Bank Rate is now the effective interest rate on roughly a quarter of the national debt. And the Asset Purchase Facility, which returned about £124 billion to the Exchequer while Bank Rate sat below the coupons it held, is now indemnified at an estimated lifetime net cost of £164 billion by the end of 2036. This paper sets out ten measures, models them as a unified plan against the OBR's March 2026 baseline to 2050-51 under five scenarios, states who bears what cost, and drafts the legislation that would be required. Every formula is written out in an appendix and the model is published in full, so the results can be checked rather than taken on trust. Use of AI tools. The analysis, the model, the figures and the argument in this paper are the author's own. A large language model was used to edit and format Part 11, the draft Bill, so that its structure, numbering and drafting conventions follow those of United Kingdom legislation. No AI tool produced any insight, analysis, interpretation or conclusion, and no AI tool is an author. The author is responsible for the whole of the text.
why: UK debt policy, off-topic for financial research.
